questions.q: Apparent volume of distribution (AVD) is defined as the:
opts: Hypothetical volume of plasma in litres necessary to account for the total amount of drug in the patient's body
Actual volume of plasma in litres measured by dilution
Volume of drug solution administered intravenously
Volume of drug distributed to adipose tissue
questions.exp: 'Hypothetical volume of plasma in litres necessary to account for the total amount of drug (intravascularly and extravascularly) in the patient's body.' (Book p9)

questions.q: In the definition of AVD, the 'total amount of drug' refers to drug present:
questions.exp: The definition specifies the total amount of drug, both intravascularly and extravascularly, in the patient's body. (Book p9)

questions.q: A drug with a high AVD is located mostly in the:
questions.exp: 'Drug with ↑AVD → mostly in Extravascular compartment/Tissue.' (Book p9)

questions.q: A drug with a low AVD is located mostly in the:
questions.exp: 'Drug with ↓AVD → mostly in Intravascular compartment/Systemic.' (Book p9)

questions.q: AVD is called 'apparent' because:
opts: It is a hypothetical volume, not a real anatomical space
It is measured directly in plasma
It is calculated only for IV drugs
questions.exp: AVD is defined as a hypothetical volume of plasma in litres needed to account for the total drug in the body, not a real measured compartment. (Book p9)

questions.q: The formula given for apparent volume of distribution is:
questions.exp: AVD = D(dose)/C0 × f, where C0 is the initial plasma concentration and f is bioavailability. (Book p9)

questions.q: In the AVD formula, C0 represents the:
questions.exp: The arrow under the formula labels C0 as 'Initial plasma concentration' — the concentration extrapolated to zero time after IV dosing. (Book p9)

questions.q: In the AVD formula, f stands for:
questions.exp: 'f: Bioavailability' — and the text notes 'f = 1 in intravenous route'. (Book p9)

questions.q: In which route is the value of f taken as 1?
questions.exp: 'f = 1 in intravenous route' — the IV route has 100% bioavailability, so f = 1. (Book p9)

questions.q: The formula given for loading dose is:
questions.exp: Loading dose: D = AVD × CT/f, where CT is the target plasma concentration. (Book p9)

questions.q: In the loading dose formula, CT is the:
questions.exp: CT is labelled 'Target plasma concentration (constant)' — the concentration we wish to achieve and maintain. (Book p9)

questions.q: As shown in the box, the loading dose is:
questions.exp: The text states 'D ∝ AVD/f': loading dose rises with a larger volume of distribution and falls with higher bioavailability. (Book p9)

questions.q: If the AVD of a drug is increased, the loading dose must be:
questions.exp: 'If AVD of a drug is ↑, Dose is increased to maintain CT' — a bigger apparent volume needs a bigger loading dose. (Book p9)

questions.q: A drug has a large AVD and low bioavailability. Its loading dose will be:
questions.exp: Since D ∝ AVD/f, a big volume of distribution and a low f both increase the required loading dose to achieve the target concentration. (Book p9)

questions.q: Which of the following is a factor determining apparent volume of distribution?
questions.exp: The factors listed are fat content, lipid solubility (pKa), albumin/plasma protein binding and tissue binding — gastric/urinary pH relate to ionisation, not distribution. (Book p9)

questions.q: In obese individuals, the volume of distribution of a drug:
questions.exp: 'Obesity: ↑ volume of distribution (vd)' — excess fat increases the compartment available to lipid-soluble drug. (Book p9)

questions.q: In athletes, the volume of distribution of a drug:
opts: Is equal to that in obesity
questions.exp: 'Athletes: ↓ vd' — athletes have less fat and more lean tissue, lowering the apparent volume of distribution for fat-soluble drugs. (Book p9)

questions.q: Regarding sex, the volume of distribution is greater in:
opts: Females, because of higher fat content
Males, because of higher fat content
Females, because of higher muscle mass
Males, because of higher muscle mass
questions.exp: 'Sex: F(↑ Fat content) > M' — women have more fat, hence a higher volume of distribution. (Book p9)

questions.q: Which drug property is listed as a determinant of AVD?
questions.exp: 'Lipid Soluble (pKa)' is listed among the factors determining AVD — a more lipid-soluble drug partitions into tissues and has a larger volume of distribution. (Book p9)

questions.q: Plasma protein (albumin) binding is related to the volume of distribution as:
questions.exp: 'Albumin binding (Plasma protein binding) ∝ 1/vd' — the more a drug is bound to plasma protein, the more it is retained intravascularly and the smaller its volume of distribution. (Book p9)

questions.q: Which factor tends to hold drug outside the plasma and thereby raise the AVD?
questions.exp: Tissue binding is listed as a factor; drug bound in tissues is not in plasma, so the apparent volume of distribution is large. (Book p9)

questions.q: A 20-year-old athlete and an obese diabetic man receive the same lipid-soluble drug. Compared with the obese man, the athlete will have:
opts: A volume of distribution equal to plasma volume
questions.exp: Obesity increases vd while athletes have a lower vd; the higher fat content of an obese individual expands the drug's apparent distribution volume. (Book p9)

questions.q: Which of the following factors would DECREASE the apparent volume of distribution of a drug?
questions.exp: Albumin binding is inversely related to vd (binding ∝ 1/vd), whereas tissue binding, obesity and lipid solubility all raise vd. (Book p9)

questions.q: The example given for pattern of distribution is that digoxin distributes to:
questions.exp: 'Distribution of Digoxin → Skeletal muscle > Heart' — the mass of skeletal muscle exceeds that of the heart. (Book p9)

questions.q: Digoxin distributes to skeletal muscle more than to the heart because of the:
opts: Greater affinity of skeletal muscle receptors
questions.exp: The diary attributes it to the greater mass ('d/t ↑ mass') of skeletal muscle compared with the heart, which is the target organ. (Book p9)

questions.q: In the digoxin example, the heart is described as the:
questions.exp: The heart is labelled '(Target organ)' while skeletal muscle, being greater in mass, becomes the main distribution site. (Book p9)

questions.q: The loading dose of digoxin is determined by:
opts: Lean body mass and not total body mass
Total body mass and not lean body mass
questions.exp: 'Hence loading dose is determined by lean body mass (not total body mass)' — fat contributes little to digoxin's distribution. (Book p9)

questions.q: A morbidly obese patient requires a digoxin loading dose. Basing the dose on total body weight would:
opts: Overdose the patient, because digoxin distributes to lean mass
Underdose the patient, because fat stores digoxin
Be correct, because fat binds digoxin
Have no effect on the dose
questions.exp: Because digoxin's loading dose is set by lean body mass and not total body mass, dosing a very obese patient on total weight would exceed the requirement. (Book p9)

questions.q: A very high AVD leads to which pair of concentration changes?
questions.exp: '↑↑vd → ↑extravascular concentration; ↓intravascular concentration' — the drug is mostly outside the plasma. (Book p9)

questions.q: Dialysis is ineffective in toxicity of drugs with a high AVD because:
opts: The drug is largely outside the vascular compartment
The drug is too large to be dialysed
The drug is bound to dialyser membranes
The drug is metabolised during dialysis
questions.exp: With a high vd the extravascular concentration is high and the intravascular concentration low, so dialysis can remove only a negligible intravascular fraction — hence the note 'Dialysis is ineffective'. (Book p9)

questions.q: In toxicity due to drugs that are not cleared by dialysis, treatment is with:
questions.exp: The text states 'Antidotes are given in toxicity' — for high-vd drugs the antidote, not dialysis, is the treatment. (Book p9)

questions.q: A patient with organophosphate poisoning has a drug with a very high vd. The appropriate management per the text is:
opts: Give the antidote atropine, as dialysis is ineffective
questions.exp: For high-vd drugs, dialysis is ineffective (low intravascular concentration) and antidotes are given — the table pairs organophosphates with atropine. (Book p9)

questions.q: The mnemonic BADDOC lists drugs with:
questions.exp: The page is headed 'Drugs with ↑ vd: mnemonic: BADDOC.' — these are the drugs that are not cleared by dialysis. (Book p10)

questions.q: In the mnemonic BADDOC, the letter 'O' stands for:
questions.exp: BADDOC = Benzodiazepines, Beta blockers, Amphetamines, Digoxin, opiOids, Calcium channel blockers; organophosphates are also listed in the table but O stands for opioids. (Book p10)

questions.q: In the mnemonic BADDOC, the letter 'C' stands for:
questions.exp: BADDOC ends with Calcium channel blockers, which are treated with calcium gluconate. (Book p10)

questions.q: In BADDOC, the two groups beginning with the letter 'B' are:
questions.exp: BADDOC = Benzodiazepines, Beta blockers, Amphetamines, Digoxin, Opioids, Calcium channel blockers. (Book p10)

questions.q: The table of drugs with ↑vd is titled 'Drugs not cleared by dialysis', and the second column lists their:
questions.exp: The two columns are 'Drugs not cleared by dialysis' and 'Antidotes' — for each high-vd drug the specific antidote is given. (Book p10)

questions.q: As per the table, the antidote for benzodiazepine toxicity is:
questions.exp: Benzodiazepines → Flumazenil in the antidote table. (Book p10)

questions.q: As per the table, the antidote for beta blocker toxicity is:
questions.exp: Beta blockers (blocks GPCR) → Glucagon (↑cAMP): glucagon raises cAMP by a non-β-receptor route, bypassing the blocked receptor. (Book p10)

questions.q: As per the table, the antidote for amphetamine toxicity is:
questions.exp: Amphetamines → Ammonium chloride, the urine acidifier that traps the basic drug for excretion. (Book p10)

questions.q: As per the table, the antidote for digoxin toxicity is:
opts: Digoxin immune Fab only by dialysis
questions.exp: Digoxin → Digibind in the antidote table; because digoxin has a high vd, dialysis would not clear it. (Book p10)

questions.q: As per the table, the antidote for opioid toxicity is:
questions.exp: Opioids → Naloxone, the opioid receptor antagonist. (Book p10)

questions.q: As per the table, the antidote for organophosphate toxicity is:
questions.exp: Organophosphates → Atropine, which reverses the muscarinic effects of the accumulated acetylcholine. (Book p10)

questions.q: As per the table, the antidote for calcium channel blocker toxicity is:
questions.exp: Calcium channel blockers → Calcium gluconate, which supplies calcium to overcome the channel blockade. (Book p10)

questions.q: Which drug-antidote pair is INCORRECTLY matched?
questions.exp: Calcium channel blockers are treated with calcium gluconate; naloxone is the antidote for opioids. (Book p10)

questions.q: A patient with beta blocker overdose is unresponsive to atropine. Which agent from the antidote table should be given?
questions.exp: The table lists beta blockers → glucagon (↑cAMP); glucagon bypasses the blocked β receptor by increasing cAMP directly. (Book p10)

questions.q: Why is haemodialysis NOT the treatment of choice in opioid overdose per this page?
opts: Opioids have a high volume of distribution and are not cleared by dialysis
Opioids are too tightly protein bound
Opioids are cleared by the lungs
questions.exp: The table places opioids in the 'drugs not cleared by dialysis' group (BADDOC, high vd), so the antidote naloxone is used instead. (Book p10)

questions.q: Which drug from BADDOC has a specific antibody fragment as its antidote?
questions.exp: The table pairs digoxin with Digibind; digoxin's large volume of distribution is why dialysis cannot clear it. (Book p10)

questions.q: A patient with benzodiazepine overdose and a high AVD is given flumazenil rather than dialysis because:
opts: Drugs in BADDOC are not cleared by dialysis
questions.exp: The table's very heading is 'Drugs not cleared by dialysis', listing benzodiazepines with flumazenil as the antidote — a direct consequence of their high volume of distribution. (Book p10)

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a member of the BADDOC group?
questions.exp: BADDOC = Benzodiazepines, Beta blockers, Amphetamines, Digoxin, Opioids, Calcium channel blockers; phenytoin is not part of this high-vd group. (Book p10)

questions.q: The most important plasma protein binding acidic drugs, and the most common binding protein, is:
questions.exp: 'Albumin → Binds to Acidic drugs (m/c)' — albumin is the commonest plasma protein that binds acidic drugs. (Book p10)

questions.q: α1 acid glycoprotein binds:
questions.exp: 'α1 acid glycoprotein: Basic drugs' — basic drugs such as lidocaine and opioids bind α1 acid glycoprotein. (Book p10)

questions.q: Which of the following is listed as a drug bound to albumin?
questions.exp: Antipsychotics are in the albumin column; lidocaine, tricyclic antidepressants and amiodarone bind α1 acid glycoprotein. (Book p10)

questions.q: The antibiotics listed in the albumin column are:
questions.exp: The albumin list includes 'Antibiotics: sulfonamides'. (Book p10)

questions.q: The anticoagulant listed as an albumin-bound drug is:
questions.exp: 'Anticoagulant: warfarin' appears in the albumin column, together with aspirin. (Book p10)

questions.q: Which set lists drugs bound to albumin as per the table?
opts: Antipsychotics, antidepressants, antiepileptics, sulfonamides, warfarin and aspirin
questions.exp: The albumin column lists antipsychotics, antidepressants, antiepileptics, antibiotics (sulfonamides), warfarin and aspirin. (Book p10)

questions.q: Which set lists drugs bound to α1 acid glycoprotein?
opts: Tricyclic antidepressants, opioids and antiarrhythmics (beta blocker, amiodarone, lidocaine)
questions.exp: The α1 acid glycoprotein column lists tricyclic antidepressants, opioids and antiarrhythmics — beta blockers, amiodarone and lidocaine. (Book p10)

questions.q: Lidocaine, amiodarone and beta blockers are bound to:
questions.exp: These three antiarrhythmics are listed under α1 acid glycoprotein, the binding protein for basic drugs. (Book p10)

questions.q: A basic drug such as an opioid will bind mainly to:
questions.exp: α1 acid glycoprotein binds basic drugs such as opioids, tricyclic antidepressants and antiarrhythmics; albumin binds acidic drugs. (Book p10)

questions.q: Which pairing of drug and binding protein is correct?
opts: Aspirin — albumin; lidocaine — α1 acid glycoprotein
Aspirin — α1 acid glycoprotein; lidocaine — albumin
Warfarin — α1 acid glycoprotein; opioids — albumin
Sulfonamides — α1 acid glycoprotein; amiodarone — albumin
questions.exp: Aspirin, warfarin, sulfonamides and antiepileptics are albumin bound (acidic drugs), while lidocaine, opioids, tricyclics and amiodarone bind α1 acid glycoprotein (basic drugs). (Book p10)

questions.q: Warfarin and aspirin used together increase each other's plasma concentration, leading to:
questions.exp: The bracket linking warfarin and aspirin reads 'Increase each others plasma conc. if used together ↓ ↑Bleeding'. (Book p10)

questions.q: Both warfarin and aspirin are bound to the same plasma protein. When given together, the result is:
opts: Increased renal excretion of the free drug
questions.exp: Because both are albumin-bound, they compete for and displace each other, raising the free (unbound) concentration — hence the increased bleeding shown in the table. (Book p10)

questions.q: As per the table, a fall in albumin produces:
opts: ↑ Free drug and ↑ risk of toxicity
↑ Free drug and ↓ risk of toxicity
questions.exp: The albumin column reads: ↓Albumin → ↑Free drug → ↑Risk of toxicity. (Book p10)

questions.q: As per the table, an increase in α1 glycoprotein produces:
questions.exp: The α1 acid glycoprotein column reads: ↑α1 glycoprotein → ↓Free drug → ↓Effect. (Book p10)

questions.q: The two plasma-protein changes have opposite clinical consequences, which are:
questions.exp: Less albumin leaves more free drug and risk of toxicity, whereas more α1 acid glycoprotein binds more drug, lowering free drug and effect. (Book p10)

questions.q: A drug is 90% bound to albumin. In a patient with hypoalbuminaemia, the fraction of free drug:
opts: Increases, raising the risk of toxicity
questions.exp: The table states that a fall in albumin raises the free drug concentration and therefore the risk of toxicity. (Book p10)

questions.q: The inverse relationship between albumin binding and volume of distribution explains why drugs that are highly albumin bound:
opts: Have a low AVD as they stay intravascular
Have a high AVD as they enter tissue
questions.exp: Albumin binding ∝ 1/vd, so a heavily albumin-bound drug remains largely in the intravascular compartment and has a low apparent volume of distribution. (Book p9)

questions.q: Which statement about plasma protein binding and drug effect is correct?
opts: Only the free (unbound) drug is active, so ↓albumin raises toxicity while ↑α1 gp lowers effect
Bound drug is the active form, so more binding means more effect
Protein binding has no relation to drug effect
↓Albumin and ↑α1 gp have the same clinical consequence
questions.exp: The table's 'effect on drugs' row shows ↓albumin → ↑free drug → ↑toxicity, and ↑α1 gp → ↓free drug → ↓effect: free drug, not bound drug, produces the effect. (Book p10)

questions.q: Which condition is listed as a cause of decreased albumin?
questions.exp: Under ↓Albumin the text lists nephrotic syndrome, CKD, liver cirrhosis and diabetes mellitus; the inflammatory states and MI belong to the ↑α1 gp list. (Book p10)

questions.q: Which set lists the causes of decreased albumin given in the table?
opts: Nephrotic syndrome, CKD, liver cirrhosis and diabetes mellitus
Rheumatoid arthritis, IBD and myocardial infarction
questions.exp: Nephrotic syndrome, CKD, liver cirrhosis and diabetes mellitus are listed as conditions with ↓Albumin. (Book p10)

questions.q: As per the table, α1 glycoprotein is increased in:
questions.exp: '↑α1 gp: Inflammatory — rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease; myocardial infarction'. (Book p10)

questions.q: Which of the following is listed under inflammatory causes of increased α1 glycoprotein?
opts: Rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease
questions.exp: Rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease are listed, along with myocardial infarction, as conditions that raise α1 glycoprotein. (Book p10)

questions.q: A patient with nephrotic syndrome is prescribed an albumin-bound drug. Compared with a healthy adult, you should expect:
opts: A higher free drug level and greater toxicity risk
A lower free drug level and reduced effect
No change in free drug level
Increased protein binding of the drug
questions.exp: Nephrotic syndrome causes ↓albumin; the table shows ↓Albumin → ↑Free drug → ↑Risk of toxicity. (Book p10)

questions.q: A patient with myocardial infarction receives lidocaine. Because α1 glycoprotein is raised in MI:
opts: Free lidocaine falls and its effect is reduced
Free lidocaine rises and toxicity occurs
questions.exp: α1 acid glycoprotein (which binds lidocaine, a basic drug) rises in MI, so free drug falls and the effect is reduced. (Book p10)

questions.q: In a patient with rheumatoid arthritis, drugs bound to α1 acid glycoprotein will show:
opts: Reduced free concentration and reduced effect
questions.exp: Rheumatoid arthritis raises α1 glycoprotein; the table shows ↑α1 gp → ↓free drug → ↓effect. (Book p10)

questions.q: Which condition is NOT associated with a fall in albumin as per the table?
questions.exp: Myocardial infarction belongs to the ↑α1 glycoprotein group, not the ↓albumin group, which comprises nephrotic syndrome, CKD, liver cirrhosis and diabetes mellitus. (Book p10)

questions.q: A patient with diabetes mellitus on a highly albumin-bound antiepileptic drug develops features of toxicity. The explanation is:
opts: Low albumin raises the free drug fraction
High α1 glycoprotein raises the free drug fraction
questions.exp: Diabetes mellitus is listed among the causes of ↓albumin; with less binding protein there is more free drug and hence a risk of toxicity. (Book p10)

questions.q: An elderly woman with liver cirrhosis is prescribed a warfarin-like albumin-bound drug. Which risk is increased?
opts: Free drug toxicity due to low albumin
Reduced effect due to high albumin
Loss of the drug in urine
questions.exp: Liver cirrhosis lowers albumin; the table shows ↓Albumin → ↑Free drug → ↑Risk of toxicity. (Book p10)

units.title: Apparent Volume of Distribution: Definition
units.guide: AVD is the hypothetical volume of plasma in litres needed to account for all the drug in the body, intravascular and extravascular. A drug with a high AVD sits mainly in tissue; one with a low AVD stays in the systemic circulation. That is why it is only an 'apparent' volume.

units.title: AVD and the Loading Dose Formulas
units.guide: AVD = D/C0 × f, where C0 is the initial plasma concentration and f is bioavailability (f = 1 for the IV route). Rearranged for practice, loading dose D = AVD × CT/f, so D ∝ AVD/f: a larger volume of distribution or lower bioavailability demands a bigger loading dose to hit the target concentration.

units.title: What Determines the Volume of Distribution?
units.guide: Fat content drives vd: obesity raises it, athletes lower it, and women have more than men because of higher fat content. Lipid solubility raises vd, albumin binding lowers it (binding ∝ 1/vd) and tissue binding raises it. The drug's own chemistry and the patient's body composition both matter.

units.title: Digoxin: Distributed to Muscle, Dosed on Lean Mass
units.guide: Digoxin leaves plasma for skeletal muscle, which outweighs the heart even though the heart is the target organ. Consequently digoxin's loading dose is calculated from lean body mass, not total body mass — dosing an obese patient on total weight overshoots.

units.title: High AVD = Dialysis Is a Waste of Time
units.guide: With a very high vd the extravascular concentration is high and intravascular concentration is low, so dialysis can clear almost none of the drug — it is ineffective. Antidotes, not dialysis, are the treatment of poisoning by such drugs.

units.title: BADDOC: Drugs With High vd, and Their Antidotes
units.guide: Remember BADDOC — Benzodiazepines, Beta blockers, Amphetamines, Digoxin, Opioids, Calcium channel blockers (with organophosphates alongside). These are not cleared by dialysis, so each has a specific antidote: flumazenil, glucagon (raises cAMP), ammonium chloride, digibind, naloxone, calcium gluconate and atropine.

units.title: Albumin vs α1 Acid Glycoprotein: Who Binds What
units.guide: Albumin is the commonest plasma protein and binds acidic drugs — antipsychotics, antidepressants, antiepileptics, sulfonamides, warfarin and aspirin. α1 acid glycoprotein binds basic drugs — tricyclic antidepressants, opioids and antiarrhythmics such as beta blockers, amiodarone and lidocaine.

units.title: Displacement: Why Warfarin Plus Aspirin Bleeds
units.guide: Warfarin and aspirin are both albumin bound. Given together they displace each other, each raising the other's plasma concentration of free drug — and the clinical result written in the margin is increased bleeding.

units.title: Low Albumin Causes Toxicity, High AGP Causes Failure
units.guide: A fall in albumin leaves more free drug and so more toxicity; a rise in α1 acid glycoprotein binds more drug and so lowers free drug and effect. The same principle explains why heavily albumin-bound drugs have a low volume of distribution — they stay in the plasma.

units.title: Clinical Applications: Nephrotic, Cirrhotic, Inflamed, Infarcted
units.guide: Albumin falls in nephrotic syndrome, CKD, liver cirrhosis and diabetes mellitus — predict toxicity of albumin-bound drugs. α1 glycoprotein rises in inflammation (rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease) and myocardial infarction — predict reduced free drug and reduced effect, as with lidocaine in MI.
